chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Lagniappe and Hinton's grandmother
summary: Hinton recalls his grandmother's Creole French.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I remember my grandmother had a lot of expressions that she brought up from Mississippi. Words like "lanyet" (PHONETIC) (laniappe)

Creole French. She would tell me to go to the store and get a dime's worth of lanyet and a nickel's worth of sweet potatoes in Mississippi. And she says, Turn the lanyet me an onion. So after I spent 15 cents, the guy would throw in an onion for her. Now, if one of my neighbors sent me to the store, she would have to give me the lanyet for going, so I could lanyet up a piece of candy. (Laughter.) And it would break my heart if this lady would ask me to go to the store and she'd tell me, tell Buck to lanyet me up an egg, and I was out of it.

She had many more, just beautiful. That's what's so remarkable about you, Jimmy, you've come through these different things and not only have you made a study of languages but you've made a study of people and been involved with so many different people and different ethnic backgrounds, and you've been able to survive and make friends with them.
